title: Why Transformers Use Multi-Head Attention
body:
A single attention mechanism can only focus on one relationship at a time, such as subject-verb agreement.

Multi-head attention splits the queries, keys, and values into multiple subspaces, allowing the model to attend to different positions simultaneously.

Observe how the two heads distribute their weights differently across the input sequence in

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Head A focuses on local syntax while Head B captures long-range context.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["the_1","cat","sat","on","the_2","mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.05,0.65,0.2,0.05,0.02,0.03]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.38,0.17,0.09,0.05,0.08,0.23]}]}}
```

. Head A concentrates heavily on the immediate subject cat, whereas Head B spreads attention across contextual markers.

By projecting inputs into separate representation subspaces, the network learns diverse features in parallel. This mechanism increases model capacity without a proportional explosion in computational complexity.

prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
title: Why Transformers Use Multi-Head Attention
body:
A transformer uses multi-head attention to look at text from multiple perspectives at the same time. If a model had only one attention head, it would average all relationships into a single compromise vector.

This averaging hides distinct linguistic patterns that happen simultaneously in a sentence.

Look at how different heads focus on separate words when querying the word sat in the bar chart below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Both heads query sat. Head A puts the most weight on cat, and Head B puts the most on the first the.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["1. the","2. cat","3. sat","4. on","5. the","6. mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.388,0.175,0.093,0.049,0.077,0.218]}]}}
```

Head A strongly focuses on the subject cat, capturing local syntactic structure. Meanwhile, Head B distributes weight across structural determiners like the, capturing broader positional context.

Multiple heads allow the model to attend to syntax, semantics, and position in parallel projections.

title: Why Transformers Use Multiple Attention Heads
body:
A transformer splits its query, key, and value vectors into multiple subspaces called attention heads to focus on different aspects of a sequence simultaneously.

Single attention heads average out relational signals, making it hard to track syntactic and semantic links at once.

Notice how the two series in the chart differ in their focus across the sentence tokens.

Head A tracks local subject-verb links, whereas Head B captures broader structural dependencies like articles. This multi-head mechanism lets the model project inputs into distinct representation spaces in parallel.

prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
title: Multi-Head Attention in Transformers
body:
Multi-head attention allows a transformer to jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

Rather than computing a single attention function, the query, key, and value matrices are projected $h$ times with different learned linear projections.

Look at the bar chart in to see how two separate attention heads assign different importance weights to the same context tokens for the word sat.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Both heads query sat. Head A puts the most weight on cat, and Head B puts the most on the first the.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["1. the","2. cat","3. sat","4. on","5. the","6. mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.388,0.175,0.093,0.049,0.077,0.218]}]}}
```

Each head learns to focus on distinct linguistic features such as syntactic structure, positional distance, or semantic coreference.

The outputs of all heads are concatenated and linearly transformed back into the expected dimension.

title: Multi-Head Attention
body:
Multi-head attention splits the $d_{\text{model}}$ hidden dimensions into $h$ separate subspaces, letting the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces at different positions.

Look at how each head distributes its weights across different tokens in the chart below.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Head A focuses on syntactic links, while Head B captures positional markers.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["the first","cat","sat","on","the second","mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.05,0.65,0.2,0.05,0.01,0.04]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.35,0.15,0.1,0.05,0.05,0.3]}]}}
```

By computing $Q_i = QW_i^Q$, $K_i = KW_i^K$, and $V_i = VW_i^V$ for each head $i$, the transformer projects inputs into diverse subspaces.

This structural design prevents a single weighted average from washing out distinct relational patterns like syntax versus proximity.

prompt: Why does a transformer use more than one attention head?
title: Multi-Head Attention
body:
Multi-head attention projects queries, keys, and values $h$ times into lower-dimensional spaces, running attention in parallel to let the model jointly attend to information from different representation subspaces.

Notice how Head A focuses on syntactic agreement with cat while Head B captures positional context from the article.

```rh-diagram
{"version":1,"diagram":{"title":"Attention weights by head and token","caption":"Both heads query sat. Head A puts the most weight on cat, and Head B puts the most on the first the.","kind":"bar-chart","variant":"grouped","categories":["1. the","2. cat","3. sat","4. on","5. the","6. mat"],"series":[{"label":"Head A","values":[0.052,0.65,0.192,0.059,0.02,0.027]},{"label":"Head B","values":[0.388,0.175,0.093,0.049,0.077,0.218]}]}}
```

Mathematically, given projections $Q W_i^Q$, $K W_i^K$, and $V W_i^V$, each head computes scaled dot-product attention independently before concatenation and linear transformation $W^O$.

Without multiple heads, a single attention distribution averages out these distinct relational roles, collapsing the richness of token interactions into one compromise vector.
